The SVD, for programmers

The theorem (full and reduced forms) and its geometric reading, the link to the eigenvalues of AᵀA and why it isn't computed that way, rank, norms and conditioning, low-rank approximation with the Eckart–Young theorem, the pseudoinverse and regularization by filters, PCA, and truncated or randomized SVD for large matrices. With a from-scratch module verified against NumPy and scikit-learn, a simulated fleet of 300 trucks and an example worked by hand.

Summary

  • Every is with , orthogonal and nonnegative diagonal: rotate, scale along axes, rotate. The unit sphere goes to a hyperellipsoid with semi-axes .
  • : the are its eigenvalues. But computing it that way squares the condition number and wipes out the below .
  • , , , and the numerical rank is the number of above a tolerance.
  • Eckart–Young: the sum of the first layers is the best rank- approximation in the 2-norm (error ) and in Frobenius (error ).
  • gives the minimum-norm least-squares solution. Truncating or using ridge are filters on the that avoid dividing noise by small numbers.
  • PCA is the SVD of the centered data. For large matrices, only the first layers: Lanczos (ARPACK) or randomized methods.

§1 · The theorem

Rotate, scale along axes, rotate

Theorem. For every there exist orthogonal matrices , and a diagonal with , , such that

The are the singular values (unique), the columns of are the right singular vectors (input directions) and the of , the left ones (output directions). There are three ways to write it, depending on how much you keep:

The compact form is the sum of rank-1 matrices, : the "layers" of the simple version. Geometry: rotates (or reflects) the unit sphere of without deforming it, scales each axis by (and drops or adds dimensions) and places the result in : the sphere ends up as a hyperellipsoid with semi-axes . It is the decomposition of the linear transformation of topic 3 into its simplest pieces.

Existence (sketch). Let , attained at some by compactness of the sphere; if , . For any unit , : otherwise, would satisfy

which exceeds for a small of the right sign. So maps to and the argument is repeated on the restriction, of lower dimension. Uniqueness: the are unique; if they are distinct, each pair is unique up to a common sign; if a is repeated, only the subspace is unique. Those arbitrary signs are why two libraries give components with different signs (§6, §7).

§2 · Eigenvalues

AᵀA and AAᵀ, and why it isn't computed that way

Substituting the decomposition:

which are orthogonal diagonalizations of two symmetric positive semidefinite matrices (topic 5): the are eigenvectors of , the of , and the nonzero eigenvalues of both are the . This gives the usual constructive proof and the by-hand method for small matrices (§10): eigenvalues of , square roots, and . For symmetric , with the same vectors (up to the sign of the negative ones). Another useful connection: the symmetric matrix has eigenvalues , and that's how Lanczos methods for sparse SVD work.

Why not in practice. Forming squares the condition number, , as with the normal equations of topic 4. A stable algorithm for eigenvalues of a symmetric matrix makes absolute errors of order in each , so the recovered is garbage as soon as , that is, . Working on , the absolute error is . With , the route is off by 4%; with , by 3,700%. Library algorithms never form : Golub–Kahan reduces to bidiagonal form with Householder reflections from both sides () and then diagonalizes with implicit QR (LAPACK gesvd) or with divide and conquer (gesdd, the one used by np.linalg.svd and, by default, scipy.linalg.svd). The cost is . The Jacobi method of §7 is slower but simple, and has very good relative accuracy (Demmel and Veselić, 1992).

§3 · What the σ tell you

Rank, norms, conditioning and the four subspaces

( for of full column rank.) All three norms are invariant under orthogonal transformations, which is why they depend only on the ; the Frobenius one follows from . The nuclear norm is the convex relaxation of rank used by matrix completion methods. Numerical rank: with floating-point data no is exactly 0; you count those above a tolerance (np.linalg.matrix_rank uses ), or look for a clear gap in the spectrum, like the one in §8. Also, is the distance (in the 2-norm) from to the nearest singular matrix: is how close is, in relative terms, to losing rank.

The four subspaces. With rank : are an orthonormal basis of ; , of its complement ; , of the row space; , of the null space . The orthogonal projector onto the column space from topic 4 is .

The Eckart–Young theorem

Truncating the sum of layers at gives , stored with numbers. Theorem (Eckart and Young, 1936; Mirsky, 1960, for every rotation-invariant norm): for ,

Proof in the 2-norm. has norm . If , its null space has dimension and meets , of dimension : there is a unit in both, and

The fraction ("energy") is . If , is not unique. In the ML series, PCA applies this theorem to centered data to justify that its components are the best projection; here it holds for any matrix, centered or not. §5 · Pseudoinverse

Minimum-norm least squares and regularization by filters

The Moore–Penrose pseudoinverse inverts what it can and zeroes the rest:

It is the only matrix that satisfies , and makes and symmetric (they are the orthogonal projectors onto and the row space). For , with :

The minimum requires for and leaves the free; setting them to 0 minimizes . So is the minimum-norm least-squares solution (with full rank, the only one). It's what np.linalg.lstsq returns (and the projection of topic 4 is ).

The problem with dividing by . If , component of the solution carries : the noise is amplified by . The classical regularizations multiply each term by a filter factor :

The truncated SVD cuts off sharply; ridge (topic 4) smoothly switches off the directions with , and is its effective degrees of freedom. Fleet example: recovering the speed (1 Hz, 2 minutes) from the GPS cumulative distance with ±3 m of noise. is the lower-triangular matrix of ones (cumulative sum), with ; undoing it is differentiating, and differentiating noise amplifies it.

regul.py · actual output

"""Speed from noisy cumulative distance: pseudoinverse, truncated SVD and ridge."""
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import Ridge
from svd import svd_jacobi

n = 120; t = np.arange(n)                                       # 2 minutes, one sample per second
v = np.interp(t, [0, 25, 55, 70, 80, 95, 119], [0, 22, 23, 9, 9, 20, 20])   # m/s: starts, roundabout, goes on
A = np.tril(np.ones((n, n)))                                    # distance = cumulative sum of speed (Δt = 1 s)
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)
b = A @ v + rng.normal(0, 3.0, n)                               # GPS: ±3 m in the distance
U, s, Vt = svd_jacobi(A)
c = U.T @ b
print(f"σ₁ = {s[0]:.1f}, σ_n = {s[-1]:.3f}, κ(A) = {s[0] / s[-1]:.0f}")
rmse = lambda x: np.sqrt(np.mean((x - v) ** 2))
x_pinv = Vt.T @ (c / s)
print(f"pseudoinverse (all layers): RMSE {rmse(x_pinv):.2f} m/s")
best_k = min(range(1, n + 1), key=lambda k: rmse(Vt[:k].T @ (c[:k] / s[:k])))
print(f"truncated SVD, best k = {best_k}: RMSE {rmse(Vt[:best_k].T @ (c[:best_k] / s[:best_k])):.2f} m/s")
lams = 10 ** np.linspace(-3, 3, 241)
xr = lambda lam: Vt.T @ (s / (s**2 + lam) * c)                   # filters σ²/(σ²+λ) applied to c/σ
best_l = min(lams, key=lambda l: rmse(xr(l)))
print(f"ridge, best λ = {best_l:.3g}: RMSE {rmse(xr(best_l)):.2f} m/s")
sk = Ridge(alpha=best_l, fit_intercept=False, solver="svd").fit(A, b).coef_
print(f"ridge via filters vs sklearn Ridge(solver='svd'): {np.abs(sk - xr(best_l)).max():.1e}")
f = s**2 / (s**2 + best_l)
print(f"filters with that λ: f₁ = {f[0]:.4f}, f_{best_k} = {f[best_k - 1]:.3f}, f_n = {f[-1]:.4f}; degrees of freedom {f.sum():.1f}")

# σ₁ = 76.7, σ_n = 0.500, κ(A) = 153
# pseudoinverse (all layers): RMSE 3.75 m/s
# truncated SVD, best k = 36: RMSE 1.16 m/s
# ridge, best λ = 1.68: RMSE 1.23 m/s
# ridge via filters vs sklearn Ridge(solver='svd'): 2.0e-12
# filters with that λ: f₁ = 0.9997, f_36 = 0.428, f_n = 0.1296; degrees of freedom 43.3

The full pseudoinverse gives 3.75 m/s of error (13.5 km/h); truncating at 36 layers or ridge with , about 1.2 m/s. Careful: here and were chosen by looking at the truth, which you don't have in practice; you choose them by cross-validation, generalized cross-validation or the L-curve criterion (Hansen, 1998).

§6 · Data

PCA via SVD, signs and large matrices

With the centered data (rows = observations), the sample covariance is : the principal components are the rows of , the variances and the scores . scikit-learn computes PCA this way (without forming , because of §2) and fixes the signs with svd_flip(u_based_decision=False): in each component, the entry with the largest absolute value is positive. The details of how many components to keep and how to interpret them are in PCA; here, just the equivalence, checked with the fleet from §8:

pca_svd.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA, TruncatedSVD
from sim import flota
from svd import svd_jacobi

X, *_ = flota()                                         # 300 trucks × 28 days
Xc = X - X.mean(axis=0)                                 # PCA: center each column (each day)
U, s, Vt = svd_jacobi(Xc)
sg = np.sign(Vt[np.arange(len(s)), np.abs(Vt).argmax(axis=1)])   # signs as in svd_flip(u_based_decision=False)
U, Vt = U * sg, Vt * sg[:, None]
p = PCA(n_components=5, svd_solver="full").fit(X)
print("components vs PCA.components_       ", f"{np.abs(Vt[:5] - p.components_).max():.1e}")
print("σ²/(n−1) vs explained_variance_      ", f"{np.max(np.abs(s[:5]**2 / (len(X) - 1) - p.explained_variance_) / p.explained_variance_):.1e}")
print("U·Σ vs PCA.transform(X)              ", f"{np.abs(U[:, :5] * s[:5] - p.transform(X)).max():.1e}")
ts = TruncatedSVD(n_components=5, algorithm="arpack").fit(X)      # not centered
media = X.mean(axis=0) / np.linalg.norm(X.mean(axis=0))
print("not centered: |cos| between the 1st component and the direction of the mean", round(abs(ts.components_[0] @ media), 4))
print("% of variance, PCA (centered):", (100 * p.explained_variance_ratio_).round(1))

# components vs PCA.components_        3.8e-15
# σ²/(n−1) vs explained_variance_       7.3e-15
# U·Σ vs PCA.transform(X)               4.3e-12
# not centered: |cos| between the 1st component and the direction of the mean 0.9992
# % of variance, PCA (centered): [87.7  7.9  1.6  0.2  0.2]

To center or not. Without centering, the first layer mostly captures the mean (cosine 0.9992 with its direction): that's what happens in the simple version, where layer 1 is "the routine". TruncatedSVD deliberately doesn't center, because centering a sparse matrix makes it dense (latent semantic analysis, recommender systems with implicit zeros). For finding anomalies by residual it doesn't matter; to talk about "explained variance", you have to center.

Large matrices. If you only care about the first layers, you don't need the full SVD. Lanczos / ARPACK (scipy.sparse.linalg.svds, TruncatedSVD(algorithm="arpack")) only needs products and , ideal for sparse matrices. Randomized methods (Halko, Martinsson and Tropp, 2011; randomized_svd, the default in TruncatedSVD) multiply by a Gaussian matrix with columns, orthonormalize the image (), apply a few power iterations to separate close and do the exact SVD of the small . The expected error is bounded in terms of and the tail of the spectrum, and is nearly the Eckart–Young error when the spectrum decays fast. Which one is faster depends on the size, the sparsity and : measure it on your own data. For data arriving in batches, IncrementalPCA updates the decomposition without loading everything into memory.

§7 · From scratch

Jacobi, power iteration with deflation, randomized and pseudoinverse, verified

One-sided Jacobi (Hestenes, 1958): look for rotations that make the columns of orthogonal; then with the norms of the columns. Each Givens rotation in the plane zeroes the dot product of those two columns: with , , , take and , the small root of . Sweep all pairs until none moves; the final convergence is quadratic. Power iteration with deflation: converges to with ratio ; subtract the layer and repeat. It's simple but slow when the are close.

svd.py

"""SVD from scratch: closed-form 2×2, one-sided Jacobi, power iteration with deflation,
randomized version, pseudoinverse and low-rank approximation."""
import numpy as np


def svd_2x2(A):
    """A = U diag(s) Vᵀ for a 2×2 A, with the angle of AᵀA in closed form."""
    A = np.asarray(A, float)
    G = A.T @ A
    teta = 0.5 * np.arctan2(2 * G[0, 1], G[0, 0] - G[1, 1])      # direction of v₁
    V = np.array([[np.cos(teta), -np.sin(teta)], [np.sin(teta), np.cos(teta)]])
    W = A @ V                                                     # orthogonal columns: σ₁u₁, σ₂u₂
    s = np.linalg.norm(W, axis=0)
    U = np.zeros((2, 2))
    U[:, 0] = W[:, 0] / s[0] if s[0] > 0 else [1.0, 0.0]
    U[:, 1] = [-U[1, 0], U[0, 0]]                                 # complete to an orthonormal basis
    if s[1] > 0 and U[:, 1] @ W[:, 1] < 0:                        # the sign goes into U (reflection), not into σ₂
        U[:, 1] *= -1
    return U, s, V.T


def _completar(U, r):
    """Complete columns r.. of U to an orthonormal basis (Gram–Schmidt with the standard basis)."""
    m = U.shape[0]
    for k in range(r, U.shape[1]):
        for e in np.eye(m):
            w = e - U[:, :k] @ (U[:, :k].T @ e)
            w = w - U[:, :k] @ (U[:, :k].T @ w)                    # second pass: reorthogonalize
            if np.linalg.norm(w) > 1e-8:
                U[:, k] = w / np.linalg.norm(w)
                break
    return U


def svd_jacobi(A, tol=1e-15, max_barridos=60):
    """Reduced SVD by one-sided Jacobi (Hestenes): rotates pairs of columns until they are orthogonal.
    Returns U (m×p), s (p), Vt (p×n) with p = min(m, n) and s in decreasing order."""
    A = np.asarray(A, float)
    m, n = A.shape
    if m < n:                                                     # work with the tall form
        U, s, Vt = svd_jacobi(A.T, tol, max_barridos)
        return Vt.T, s, U.T
    W = A.copy(); V = np.eye(n)
    for _ in range(max_barridos):
        quieto = True
        for p in range(n - 1):
            for q in range(p + 1, n):
                a, b = W[:, p] @ W[:, p], W[:, q] @ W[:, q]
                c = W[:, p] @ W[:, q]
                if abs(c) <= tol * np.sqrt(a * b) or c == 0:
                    continue
                quieto = False
                z = (b - a) / (2 * c)                                 # rotation that zeroes the dot product
                t = np.sign(z) / (abs(z) + np.sqrt(1 + z * z)) if z != 0 else 1.0
                cs = 1 / np.sqrt(1 + t * t); sn = cs * t
                Wp, Wq = W[:, p].copy(), W[:, q].copy()
                W[:, p], W[:, q] = cs * Wp - sn * Wq, sn * Wp + cs * Wq
                Vp, Vq = V[:, p].copy(), V[:, q].copy()
                V[:, p], V[:, q] = cs * Vp - sn * Vq, sn * Vp + cs * Vq
        if quieto:
            break
    s = np.linalg.norm(W, axis=0)
    o = np.argsort(-s, kind="stable"); s, W, V = s[o], W[:, o], V[:, o]
    r = int(np.sum(s > max(m, n) * np.finfo(float).eps * (s[0] if len(s) else 0)))
    U = np.zeros((m, n)); U[:, :r] = W[:, :r] / s[:r]
    s[r:] = 0.0
    return _completar(U, r), s, V.T


def potencia_deflacion(A, k, iters=500, tol=1e-13, seed=0):
    """The first k layers by power iteration on AᵀA, subtracting each layer found."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    R = np.array(A, float); m, n = R.shape
    U, s, Vt = np.zeros((m, k)), np.zeros(k), np.zeros((k, n))
    for j in range(k):
        v = rng.normal(size=n); v /= np.linalg.norm(v); sig = 0.0
        for _ in range(iters):
            w = R.T @ (R @ v)                                     # one power step with AᵀA, without forming it
            nw = np.linalg.norm(w)
            if nw == 0:
                break
            v_nuevo = w / nw
            if np.linalg.norm(v_nuevo - v) < tol:
                v = v_nuevo; break
            v = v_nuevo
        u = R @ v; sig = np.linalg.norm(u)
        u = u / sig if sig > 0 else u
        U[:, j], s[j], Vt[j] = u, sig, v
        R -= sig * np.outer(u, v)                                 # deflation: remove the layer
    return U, s, Vt


def svd_aleatorizada(A, k, sobremuestreo=10, potencias=2, seed=0):
    """Halko, Martinsson and Tropp (2011): project onto k + p random directions, orthonormalize and
    do the exact SVD of a small matrix."""
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    A = np.asarray(A, float)
    Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(A @ rng.normal(size=(A.shape[1], k + sobremuestreo)))
    for _ in range(potencias):                                    # subspace iterations: separate the σ better
        Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(A.T @ Q)
        Q, _ = np.linalg.qr(A @ Q)
    Ub, s, Vt = svd_jacobi(Q.T @ A)                               # (k + p) × n: small
    return (Q @ Ub)[:, :k], s[:k], Vt[:k]


def rango(A, rtol=None):
    _, s, _ = svd_jacobi(A)
    rtol = max(np.shape(A)) * np.finfo(float).eps if rtol is None else rtol
    return int(np.sum(s > rtol * s[0])) if s[0] > 0 else 0


def pinv(A, rtol=None):
    """Pseudoinverse A⁺ = V Σ⁺ Uᵀ: inverts the large σ and sets the rest to 0."""
    U, s, Vt = svd_jacobi(A)
    rtol = max(np.shape(A)) * np.finfo(float).eps if rtol is None else rtol
    keep = s > rtol * s[0] if s[0] > 0 else np.zeros_like(s, bool)
    return (Vt[keep].T / s[keep]) @ U[:, keep].T


def rango_k(A, k):
    """Best rank-k approximation (Eckart–Young): sum of the first k layers σᵢ uᵢ vᵢᵀ."""
    U, s, Vt = svd_jacobi(A)
    return (U[:, :k] * s[:k]) @ Vt[:k]


def normas(A):
    """2-norm (σ₁), Frobenius (square root of the sum of σ²) and condition number σ₁/σ_min."""
    _, s, _ = svd_jacobi(A)
    return s[0], np.sqrt(np.sum(s**2)), (s[0] / s[-1] if s[-1] > 0 else np.inf)

Everything matches NumPy and scikit-learn to rounding level. Details needed to make it match: comparisons of and are done up to sign (absolute value of the cosine between components) or with objects that don't depend on the sign, such as , and the norms. When , is not unique and is excluded from the comparison. The pseudoinverse uses the same tolerance as np.linalg.pinv in practice (); its error is measured multiplied by to make it relative. In the randomized version, the test matrix has clear gaps between the , so the two implementations (with different random generators) reach the same subspace; with a flat spectrum they would need more power iterations.

§8 · In the fleet

300 trucks × 28 days: three layers, noise and 20 odd days

We simulate the daily km of 120 long-haul trucks, 100 regional and 80 delivery trucks over four weeks. The truth has rank 3: the weekly routine (all of them), delivery (more Saturday, less Monday; only the 80 city trucks) and an alternating-week rotation (40 long-haul trucks). On top of that, ±25 km of noise and 20 anomalies: 10 breakdowns (a weekday at 30–50%), 6 Sunday trips of 150 to 250 km and 4 GPS jumps (km × 1.6).

sim.py

"""Simulator for the fleet in §8: daily km of 300 trucks over 4 weeks (28 days, starting on a Monday)."""
import numpy as np


def flota(seed=7, n_anom=20):
    rng = np.random.default_rng(seed)
    d = np.arange(28); dow = d % 7; sem = d // 7
    p = np.select([dow < 4, dow == 4, dow == 5], [1.0, 0.9, 0.35], 0.03)        # weekly routine
    q = np.select([dow == 5, dow == 0], [1.0, -0.35], 0.0)                         # delivery: Saturday yes, Monday light
    r = np.where(dow < 5, np.where(sem % 2 == 0, 1.0, -1.0), 0.0)                 # alternating-week rotation
    tipo = np.r_[np.zeros(120, int), np.ones(100, int), 2 * np.ones(80, int)]      # long haul, regional, delivery
    a = np.select([tipo == 0, tipo == 1], [rng.uniform(520, 640, 300), rng.uniform(350, 450, 300)], rng.uniform(150, 230, 300))
    b = np.where(tipo == 2, rng.uniform(180, 240, 300), 0.0)
    c = np.zeros(300); c[:40] = rng.uniform(120, 180, 40)                           # 40 long-haul trucks rotate
    verdad = np.outer(a, p) + np.outer(b, q) + np.outer(c, r)
    X = np.clip(verdad + rng.normal(0, 25, verdad.shape), 0, None)
    anom = np.zeros(X.shape, bool)
    filas = rng.choice(300, n_anom, replace=False)
    for k, i in enumerate(filas):
        if k < 10:                                                                 # breakdown: half a day stopped
            j = rng.choice(np.where(dow < 5)[0]); X[i, j] *= rng.uniform(0.3, 0.5)
        elif k < 16:                                                               # Sunday trip
            j = rng.choice(np.where(dow == 6)[0]); X[i, j] = rng.uniform(150, 250)
        else:                                                                      # GPS jumps: km × 1.6
            j = rng.choice(np.where(dow < 5)[0]); X[i, j] *= 1.6
        anom[i, j] = True
    return np.round(X), verdad, anom, tipo

flota.py · actual output

import numpy as np
from sim import flota
from svd import svd_jacobi

X, verdad, anom, tipo = flota()
U, s, Vt = svd_jacobi(X)
e = s**2 / np.sum(s**2)
print("σ₁…σ₈:", s[:8].round(0))
print("% of ‖X‖²_F per layer:", " ".join(f"{x:.2f}" for x in 100 * e[:6]), "  cumulative with 3:", round(100 * e[:3].sum(), 2))
ok = ~anom
print("RMSE against the truth (normal cells); raw data:", round(np.sqrt(np.mean((X - verdad)[ok] ** 2)), 1))
for k in range(1, 7):
    Xk = (U[:, :k] * s[:k]) @ Vt[:k]
    print(f"  k={k}: RMSE {np.sqrt(np.mean((Xk - verdad)[ok] ** 2)):5.1f}   ‖X − X_k‖₂ = {np.linalg.norm(X - Xk, 2):7.1f} = σ_{k + 1} {s[k]:7.1f}")

def top(score, n=20):
    o = np.argsort(-score.ravel())[:n]; return anom.ravel()[o].sum()

k = 3; Xk = (U[:, :k] * s[:k]) @ Vt[:k]; R = X - Xk
print("anomalies among the 20 cells with largest |residual| (k=3):", top(np.abs(R)), "of 20")
# naive baseline: distance to the median of the same truck on the same day of the week
dow = np.arange(28) % 7
med = np.stack([np.median(X[:, dow == w], axis=1) for w in range(7)], 1)[:, dow]
print("baseline: |km − truck's median on that weekday|:", top(np.abs(X - med)), "of 20")
# what do the layers capture? mean intensity of each layer by truck type
for j in range(3):
    sg = np.sign(Vt[j].sum()) or 1.0
    print(f"layer {j + 1}: pattern (Mon wk 1 … Sun wk 2)", (sg * Vt[j, :14] / np.abs(Vt[j]).max()).round(2),
          " mean intensity by type:", [round(float(sg * (U[tipo == t, j] * s[j]).mean() * np.abs(Vt[j]).max())) for t in range(3)])

The spectrum tells you the rank. After there is a jump to , and from there on the decrease slowly: that's the noise level (a noise matrix with standard deviation 25 has its largest near ). Three layers capture 99.56% of , and each measured is exactly .

Removing noise. The raw data are 24.2 km (RMSE) away from the noise-free truth; is 9.7 km away. With fewer layers, structure is missing (60.6 and 40.9 km); with more, noise creeps back in (11.2, 12.5…).

Individual layers versus the subspace. Layer 1 is clean: the routine, with mean intensity 619, 426 and 197 km for each type. Layers 2 and 3 mix delivery and rotation, because and are close (4,193 and 3,705) and any rotation within their plane is almost equally good. What is well determined is the subspace of the three, not each layer: don't name them without looking.

Anomalies by residual. Among the 20 cells with the largest , 18 are injected anomalies. The naive baseline, comparing each day with the median of the same truck on the same day of the week, finds 10: it doesn't know that 40 trucks alternate weeks or that delivery has its own pattern, and it flags normal days. The SVD learns those patterns from the whole fleet. Anomalies also pull on the layers (in the simple version, with 3 layers the stopped truck stops standing out); with many anomalies, there are robust versions, such as robust PCA, that separate a low-rank part and a sparse part.

§9 · Checklist

Before you trust an SVD

  • Never compute the SVD via the eigenvalues of if the small matter; use np.linalg.svd, scipy.linalg.svd or a truncated solver.
  • Scale columns with different units (or standardize) first: the SVD is not invariant to the scale of the columns.
  • Decide whether to center: for variance and PCA, yes; for sparse matrices and recommender systems, usually not.
  • Choose by looking at the spectrum (gap, noise level) or by validation, not with a fixed energy percentage applied blindly.
  • Don't interpret individual layers when their are similar: only the subspace is stable. Fix the signs (as svd_flip does) if you compare runs.
  • To solve systems, use lstsq/pinv with a deliberate tolerance (rcond) or a filter (truncation, ridge) chosen by validation.
  • For anomalies by residual: few layers, and repeat the fit without the oddest cells if they contaminate the layers.
  • With large matrices, truncated SVD (ARPACK or randomized) with a fixed seed, and check the with more iterations or more oversampling.

§10 · Worked example

A 2×2 matrix and a table of 3 trucks

The SVD of the "example" matrix from the toy in the simple version, step by step via , and the rank-1 approximation of a 3 × 2 table with its error, by hand.

The setup. The fleet analyst wants to understand what a two-variable transformation does before applying it to millions of rows, and to check with a tiny table that "keeping the first layer" loses exactly what the theory says.

Example map

First the "example" matrix from the toy in the simple version, whose columns are (2, −1) and (2, 2): we work out by hand its two singular values, its input and output directions and the two rotation angles. Then a table of 3 trucks × 2 days: its first layer, what it means and how much is lost by keeping only that layer.

  1. The matrix and the calculation to do.
  2. AᵀA: dot products between columns.
  3. The eigenvalues of AᵀA and the singular values.
  4. The input directions v₁ and v₂.
  5. The output directions u₁ and u₂, and the check.
  6. A table of 3 trucks: its AᵀA and its σ.
  7. The first layer: routine times intensity.
  8. What's lost: the error is σ₂.

  1. The matrix and the calculation to do

    In words

    We want to write as "rotate, stretch, rotate": . The by-hand route for a small matrix is: (1) compute ; (2) its eigenvalues are the ; (3) its eigenvectors are the input directions ; (4) each output direction is .

    The data

    Why go through AᵀA?

    Because : the output rotations cancel out () and what's left is a symmetric matrix whose eigenvalues (topic 5) are the squared stretches. For a 2 × 2 it's the fastest way by hand; with real data it isn't done this way, because it loses precision in the small (§2).

  2. AᵀA: dot products between columns

    The math (columns a = (2, −1) and b = (2, 2))

    What is each number?

    Each entry of is the dot product of two columns of (topic 2): on the diagonal, the squared lengths of the two transformed arrows ( and ); off the diagonal, how much they point in the same direction. If the columns were perpendicular, there would be a 0 off the diagonal and nothing to rotate at the start.

  3. The eigenvalues of AᵀA and the singular values

    In words

    For a 2 × 2, the eigenvalues satisfy . The trace is the sum of the diagonal, and the determinant is that of .

    The math

    Two checks

    : the area factor is the product of the stretches. And is the sum of the squares of all the entries of (4 + 4 + 1 + 4): it's . The 36 is , because .

    What it means: no arrow of length 1 comes out longer than 3 or shorter than 2. They are the two big numbers in the toy.

  4. The input directions v₁ and v₂

    The math: solve (AᵀA − λI) v = 0

    Where does the √5 come from?

    Any multiple of (1, 2) works as an eigenvector; we choose the one of length 1, dividing by , because has to be a rotation (columns of length 1). : they are perpendicular, as always for a symmetric matrix. The sign is free: (−1, −2) would work just as well.

    What it means: the direction that stretches the most points at 63.4°. The toy's first rotation, , takes it to the horizontal axis: it rotates (clockwise).

  5. The output directions u₁ and u₂, and the check

    The math: u = A v / σ

    Checking one entry

    . The top-left entry:

    The other three come out the same way: (2, 2, −1, 2). and are perpendicular and of length 1, so is a rotation of ; since , no reflection is needed.

    What it means: the toy's recipe with "example" is rotate , stretch × 3 and × 2, rotate . The two angles add up to because and are mirror images across the diagonal: a coincidence of this matrix, not a rule.

  6. A table of 3 trucks: its AᵀA and its σ

    In words

    Now a data table: kilometers (in hundreds) of three trucks on a Monday and a Saturday. It has 3 rows and 2 columns, so it has 2 singular values. Same method.

    The data (hundreds of km)

    truckMondaySaturday
    A86
    B63
    C64

    Where do the numbers come from?

    Each entry of is a dot product between the columns "Monday" (8, 6, 6) and "Saturday" (6, 3, 4). 197 = 136 + 61 is the trace: the sum of the squares of the six numbers in the table. 196 = 136·61 − 90·90 = 8,296 − 8,100 is the determinant of . The roots of are 196 and 1 because 196 + 1 = 197 and 196 × 1 = 196.

    What it means: one stretch of 14 and another of 1. Since what's lost is measured with , the first layer captures of the table.

  7. The first layer: routine times intensity

    The math

    Where does each factor come from?

    gives length 1. is , so there's no need to compute separately (its length is , the , with ). And carries in the denominator.

    What it means: the pattern (3, 2) says "for every 3 parts Monday, 2 parts Saturday": the common routine. Each row of is that routine times an intensity: (A), (B) and (C), that is, . Truck C follows the routine exactly: its row doesn't change.

  8. What's lost: the error is σ₂

    The math

    Why did it have to come out as σ₂?

    By Eckart–Young (§4): the error of the best rank-1 approximation, measured as the square root of the sum of squares, is the square root of the sum of the dropped . Here only is dropped. Also, is the second layer: it has rank 1 and its pattern is , perpendicular to (3, 2).

    What it means: with a single layer (2 + 3 + 1 = 6 numbers, the same as the table: with tables this small nothing is saved) the total error is 100 km, split like this: truck A drives 31 km less on Monday and 46 km more on Saturday than its routine says, and truck B the other way around. No other rank-1 table gets closer.

ejemplo.py · reproduces the numbers above

import numpy as np
from svd import svd_jacobi, rango_k

A = np.array([[2.0, 2.0], [-1.0, 2.0]])
G = A.T @ A; print(G, np.trace(G), round(np.linalg.det(G), 9))           # AᵀA, trace and determinant
lam = np.roots([1, -np.trace(G), np.linalg.det(G)]); print(lam, np.sqrt(lam))
v1 = np.array([1, 2]) / np.sqrt(5); v2 = np.array([-2, 1]) / np.sqrt(5)
print(G @ v1 / v1, G @ v2 / v2)                                          # eigenvectors: G v = λ v
u1 = A @ v1 / 3; u2 = A @ v2 / 2; print(u1 * np.sqrt(5), u2 * np.sqrt(5), round(u1 @ u2, 12))
U = np.c_[u1, u2]; V = np.c_[v1, v2]; print((U * [3, 2]) @ V.T)          # U Σ Vᵀ = A
print(np.degrees(np.arctan2(v1[1], v1[0])).round(2), np.degrees(np.arctan2(u1[1], u1[0])).round(2), np.linalg.det(A).round(9))
print(np.linalg.svd(A)[1], np.abs(svd_jacobi(A)[0].T @ U).round(12))     # same σ; same columns up to sign

B = np.array([[8.0, 6.0], [6.0, 3.0], [6.0, 4.0]])
H = B.T @ B; print(H, np.trace(H), round(np.linalg.det(H), 9), np.roots([1, -np.trace(H), np.linalg.det(H)]))
w1 = np.array([3, 2]) / np.sqrt(13); print(B @ w1 * np.sqrt(13), np.linalg.norm(B @ w1))
B1 = np.outer(B @ w1, w1); print(B1.round(4), (B1 * 13).round(9))
E = B - B1; print((E * 13).round(9) + 0.0, np.linalg.norm(E, "fro").round(12), np.linalg.norm(E, 2).round(12))
print(np.abs(rango_k(B, 1) - B1).max() < 1e-12, round(196 / 197 * 100, 2))

What would change in a real system

  • It isn't computed via AᵀA: with 2 × 2 it's harmless, but with nearly dependent columns the small σ are lost (§2).
  • Tables with thousands of rows: only the first layers, with a truncated method (§6).
  • Units: if one column were in meters and another in kilometers, layer 1 would be almost only the meters one. Scale first.
  • Choose k with the spectrum or with validation, and look at what's left out: that's where the anomalies are.
